seoTitle: Michigan Medical Malpractice Lawyer – Deadlines, Caps & Proof
seoDescription: Harmed by a doctor or hospital in Michigan? ATLAW explains the 2-year deadline, the Notice of Intent, the damages cap, and what it takes to prove a case. Free review.
tagline: Michigan makes malpractice cases harder to bring than any other injury claim. Here are the rules, the deadlines, and what a winnable case looks like.

c.v: Michigan has built more obstacles into medical malpractice claims than into any other kind of injury case: a two-year deadline instead of three, a mandatory notice to the doctor six months before you can sue, a sworn expert affidavit that has to be filed with the complaint, strict rules about which experts can testify, and a cap on pain-and-suffering damages. None of that means you cannot win. It means the case has to be built correctly from the first week, and it means that a lawyer who takes malpractice cases occasionally is at a disadvantage against hospital defense firms who do nothing else.
This page explains each rule plainly so you can judge whether what happened to you or your family member is a case worth pursuing, and what it will take.

ATLAW is a personal injury firm in Dearborn. In 13 years the firm has handled more than 10,000 cases and recovered more than $100 million for clients across Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, and Washtenaw counties. Malpractice cases are handled on contingency: no fee unless we recover money for you, and the first conversation is free.

sections.heading: What medical malpractice is, and what it is not

c.v: Malpractice is not a bad outcome. Medicine has bad outcomes without anyone being at fault. Malpractice is a bad outcome caused by a provider who failed to do what a reasonably competent provider in the same specialty would have done in the same circumstances. Michigan law (MCL 600.2912a) requires you to prove four things:

items.v: : what a reasonably prudent doctor, nurse, or hospital in that specialty would have done. For a specialist, the standard is national; for a general practitioner, it is the standard in the same or a similar community.
: the provider did something different, or failed to do what the standard required.

: the breach, more likely than not, caused the injury. Michigan requires proof that the patient would have had a better outcome, not merely a chance of one (MCL 600.2912a(2)). This is where many cases are lost.
: a real injury with real consequences.

items.v: : cancer, stroke, heart attack, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, appendicitis. The question is whether earlier diagnosis would have changed the outcome.
: wrong site, retained instruments, nerve or organ damage, anesthesia errors.

: discharged patients who were having a stroke or a heart attack.

sections.heading: The Michigan malpractice rules that decide whether you can sue

c.v: A malpractice lawsuit must be filed within two years of the act or omission (MCL 600.5805(8)). If you could not reasonably have discovered the injury within those two years, you have six months from the date you discovered it or should have (MCL 600.5838a(2)), but never more than six years after the act, except for cases involving a retained foreign object, fraud, or injury to the reproductive system. For a minor under eight, the deadline runs to the tenth birthday (MCL 600.5851(7)). For a death, the estate’s representative has additional time under MCL 600.5852, but the six-year outer limit still applies.

Before you can file, you must serve every provider you intend to sue with a written Notice of Intent at least 182 days before the complaint (MCL 600.2912b). The notice must state the facts, the standard of care you claim was breached, how it was breached, what should have been done instead, and how the breach caused the injury. Serving the notice pauses the two-year clock for the 182 days (MCL 600.5856(c)), but only if the notice is served before the deadline runs. The provider has 154 days to respond. In practice, this means a malpractice lawyer needs to be retained well inside the two years, because the records have to be obtained and reviewed by an expert before the notice can be written.

The complaint must be filed with a sworn affidavit from a qualified medical expert stating the standard of care, the breach, what should have been done, and causation (MCL 600.2912d). A complaint filed without it is subject to dismissal.

Michigan’s expert rule (MCL 600.2169) is among the strictest in the country. The expert must practice or teach in the same specialty as the defendant, and if the defendant is board-certified, the expert must be too. During the year before the malpractice, the expert must have spent most of their professional time practicing or teaching that specialty. A case against a board-certified emergency physician needs a board-certified emergency physician, not a general surgeon or an internist. Finding and paying that expert is part of what a malpractice lawyer does, and it is why a malpractice case costs tens of thousands of dollars to bring.

Michigan caps non-economic damages (pain, suffering, loss of enjoyment of life) in malpractice cases (MCL 600.1483). The cap is adjusted each January by the Michigan Treasury. For 2026 it is $596,400 for most cases and $1,065,000 for the most severe injuries: permanent loss of a limb’s function from brain or spinal cord injury, permanent cognitive impairment that prevents independent living, or permanent loss of reproductive ability.
2026 figures against the Treasury memo before publishing; 2025 was $586,300 / $1,047,000, 2024 was $569,000 / $1,016,000
There is no cap on economic damages: medical bills, lost earnings, and the cost of future care, which in a catastrophic case can run to many millions.
If the patient’s own conduct (ignoring instructions, missing follow-ups) contributed, the recovery is reduced by that share, and non-economic damages are barred above 50% (MCL 600.2959).

sections.heading: Do you have a malpractice case? An honest checklist

c.v: You may have a case if:

items.v: The injury is serious and lasting, or someone died.
A provider missed, delayed, or got wrong something that another provider later identified.
The harm would likely have been avoided with correct care.
It happened within the last two years (or you discovered it within the last six months).
The outcome was bad but the care was within the range of reasonable judgment.
The injury was minor or has resolved.
More than two years have passed and the injury was discoverable earlier.
The only harm is that you are unhappy with how you were treated, with no physical injury.

c.v: Not every medical malpractice situation results in a viable legal claim. ATLAW evaluates the circumstances and available medical records to determine whether there are grounds to pursue a case. If your situation does not support a viable claim, we will explain why.

faqs.question: How long do I have to sue for medical malpractice in Michigan?

answer.v: Two years from the malpractice (MCL 600.5805(8)), or six months from when you discovered it if it could not have been discovered sooner, with a six-year outer limit. Because the Notice of Intent must be served 182 days before filing and requires expert review first, the practical deadline for contacting a lawyer is much earlier than two years.

faqs.question: What is a Notice of Intent?

answer.v: A written notice, required by MCL 600.2912b, that you must serve on each provider at least 182 days before filing suit. It sets out the standard of care, the breach, and causation. Serving it on time pauses the statute of limitations during the waiting period.

faqs.question: Does Michigan cap medical malpractice damages?

answer.v: Yes, for non-economic damages only: $596,400 for most cases and $1,065,000 for the most severe permanent injuries in 2026, adjusted each January (MCL 600.1483). Economic damages, including future care, are not capped.

faqs.question: Do I need an expert to sue?

answer.v: Yes. Michigan requires a sworn Affidavit of Merit from a qualified expert when the complaint is filed (MCL 600.2912d), and the expert must practice in the same specialty as the defendant (MCL 600.2169). The firm finds and pays the expert.

faqs.question: Can I sue a hospital, or only the doctor?

answer.v: Both, depending on the facts. A hospital is liable for its employees (nurses, technicians, employed physicians) and for its own failures (staffing, systems, credentialing). Many physicians in Michigan hospitals are independent contractors, which affects who is named; the records show which.

faqs.question: My family member died. Can we sue?

answer.v: A wrongful death claim based on malpractice is brought by the estate’s personal representative, under the same malpractice rules and cap, with additional time under MCL 600.5852. The family recovers economic losses and loss of companionship.

faqs.question: How much does a malpractice lawyer cost?

answer.v: Nothing up front. ATLAW advances the costs of records and expert review and works on a contingency fee within Michigan’s one-third cap, set in writing before we start. You owe no fee unless we recover money for you.

faqs.question: How do I get my medical records?

answer.v: Request them in writing from each provider under Michigan’s Medical Records Access Act. Providers must respond within 30 days and may charge a regulated fee. We request them for you once retained.

faqs.question: What if the hospital was a VA or the University of Michigan?

answer.v: Different rules. VA claims are federal (Federal Tort Claims Act), with an administrative claim within two years and no jury. University of Michigan claims go through the Michigan Court of Claims with a notice requirement. Tell us where the care was given in the first call.

faqs.question: How long will the case take?

answer.v: Two to four years is typical. The Notice of Intent period alone is six months, and expert discovery is extensive. Cases that settle after the expert phase resolve faster; cases that go to trial take longer.
